item.title: Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication
item.description:
For years, she thought she was simply “too sensitive.” Crowded stores felt exhausting. Bright lights were distracting. Conversations in groups felt overwhelming, and she often replayed them in her mind afterward, wondering if she had said the wrong thing. Many women spend years believing they are shy, anxious, or “too much,” only to discover later in life that Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may help explain experiences they have had since childhood.

Autism in women is often diagnosed at a much later age because the signs are either missed or diagnosed under different ailments (1). But when a woman does receive a diagnosis of ASD, there is promising research for treatments that do not rely as heavily on medication.

What Is Autism Spectrum Disorder?

ASD is a developmental, neurodivergent condition that involves significant challenges in communication and social interaction, as well as limitations in behavior patterns. This includes repetitive, highly limited or restricted interests, and inflexibility, among others. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria were updated by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022.

If you think you or a loved one may have ASD but have yet to be diagnosed, we recommend seeing a licensed therapist in one of our offices to discuss your concerns.

Why Autism in Women Gets Missed

There are several reasons a girl may be categorized as “normal” or as having a shy personality or possibly diagnosed with anxiety instead of autism when she’s growing up.

One reason is that anyone — female or male — who is naturally less expressive will not exhibit the expressive signs of another more overt personality who is struggling with social interaction. Another reason is that some of the research used to set the gold standard of autism measures was set using boys as the model, and girls present differently (1).

While a boy with autism may be flagged for an evaluation because he limits his toys to dinosaurs and stacks them repeatedly, a girl may not be flagged because she is playing with her dolls. However, what a teacher or parent might not notice is that within her pretend play, the girl is also exhibiting behavioral patterns that would signify the need for further assessment.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

References
1. Dolfi, A., & Tudose, C. (2025). Diagnostic challenges of autism spectrum disorder in women without intellectual or language impairments: a narrative review. Journal of Medicine and Life, 18(8), 710.
2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

References

  • Yehuda, R., & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: Putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry, 17(3), 243–257. https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.20568
  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735
  • Narayan, A. J., Lieberman, A. F., & Masten, A. S. (2021). Intergenerational transmission and prevention of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Clinical Psychology Review, 85, 101997.

item.title: How Shame Therapy Can Unmask Issues Surrounding Self-Esteem
item.description:
In every episode of the classic cartoon Scooby-Doo, there is a supernatural monster that commits a crime and causes havoc in unsuspecting communities. A gang of young characters must follow the clues to solve these mysteries. They always end up exposing the villain to be an ordinary person in an elaborate costume. Similarly, shame therapy can expose the beliefs behind and beneath some of your greatest struggles and character flaws, if you are brave enough to allow it to do so.

Shame is one of the most complex emotions a person can feel, and it most often begins in childhood. No child can fully understand or process their emotions, even when they are pleasant, much less when they are attached to trauma, neglect, or abuse. People learn from a young age to push shame deep below the surface, out of sight, so that it won’t affect them.

Unfortunately, shame affects you potentially more than any other emotion, even when hidden behind a mask. It is only with shame therapy that you can begin to follow the clues that will eventually result in you unmasking and apprehending shame in your life.

Cracked Foundations

To use another metaphor, sometimes shame is like a seemingly harmless crack that appears in the walls of a building, spreading slowly across the entire wall over time. What might seem like a superficial problem that is easily covered with plaster and paint often tells of a more serious issue deep below the ground.

The appearance of a crack in the walls shows that the foundations have begun to shift or sink, potentially compromising the structural integrity of the entire building and signaling danger to its occupants. Similarly, a person’s behavior can show that they have an issue with their foundational self-beliefs and that their behaviors may be rooted in shame.

This is apparent in men who become violently angry at others for seemingly no reason. They move around life as balls of pent-up aggression and hostility, attacking anyone who dares challenge their identity or values. Like the crack that forms on the wall, their attitude and behavior suggest that they have some serious structural damage at the foundation of their identity.

Shame therapy might expose that they feel inferior because of an aspect of their personality that they feel helpless to resolve, like their height, weight, stature, or masculinity. These core components of their self-worth are so shrouded by guilt, shame, and fear that they default to displays of aggression and intimidation, rather than begin the difficult work of processing their damaged emotions.

How Shame Therapy Works

Shame therapy takes you back to your foundational experiences, to the times when you first felt cast aside, rejected, overlooked, bullied, or abused. These were the moments when your childlike mind could not understand why you were being treated a certain way and defaulted to taking the blame for the injustice.

You told yourself, maybe not with words but with beliefs, that you deserved the beating, that it was your fault the once-trusted adult did that to you, or that you were ignored all day by the parents who could do no wrong in your eyes. As a child, you were surviving.

There was no way you could understand any of these events, so you tried your best to forget them. Over time, their memory got buried underground, where you thought it would eventually be forgotten for good. What remained, however, was the narrative surrounding each of these moments. Kids might not be able to process complex emotions, but they do know how to tell a story. The stories you told yourself about the things you went through became foundational to your identity, and as foundational as the memories you buried. Shame therapy attempts to uncover and expose as many of these beliefs and stories as possible, to confront them, and to contradict them.

For example, you might have been punished by your parents when you were a child for being lazy. In a shame therapy session, you may relive that exact moment with your therapist and uncover the emotions behind the memory, even though they were buried because they were difficult to deal with. Now, in a safe place as an adult with a trusted friend, you can look at that memory again, confront it, and contradict it.

You might remember your father beating you because you hadn’t done your homework. He called you lazy, and you have had that memory in your head every time you relaxed or did not complete a task. Not only do you remember the words your father used in that moment, but you remember the fear you felt, the surprise at your father’s sudden aggression, and most of all, the guilt and shame you felt. Lazy became an identity marker for you after that because you believed what your dad told you, because, in your young eyes, he could not lie.

In shame therapy, you will be asked to think of all the times you were not lazy. You will recall each achievement, even if there are few. You will be asked if you think of other people as lazy when you see them resting, or if you would beat your own child for not finishing their homework. The likely answer is that no, you don’t think of other people as lazy, and you wouldn’t ever beat your child. Simply admitting this is a confrontation with a shame-rooted belief that has been affecting you your entire life.

By reliving painful memories like this, you are waking them and bringing them to the surface, where you can properly address them. Though they might cause you pain to remember them, or make you wince with embarrassment, those emotions begin to dissolve as you expose them to logic, truth, and self-kindness.

Sometimes your therapist will ask you to remember a powerful, emotional memory that contradicts the shameful one, such as a time when you were praised, celebrated, and felt loved. If the fruit of shame is low self-esteem, then the opposite of shame is self-kindness and self-acceptance.

A Safe Place

Everyone has unconscious beliefs about themselves and others that they have carried from childhood, sometimes into old age. You might not know that you have these beliefs, where they came from, or just how incorrect they may be. These are things that get exposed in shame therapy.

Somewhere in your youth, you heard something about yourself, you believed it, and you internalized it. It sank down to become a stone in the foundation of your identity. Now it lies there hidden, but an essential aspect of your identity and worldview.

Now you must learn that it is safe to disagree with these things, even if they have been a crucial part of how you understand the world. Sometimes in shame therapy, you will be guided through remembering a particular shameful memory, and your therapist will ask you to imagine having a friend there with you in that moment. Instantly, the idea of having a loved one there with you in that moment may flood you with warmth and a feeling of safety.

You will be asked to imagine your friend’s response to the situation, or what they would do to protect you. Ultimately, you will feel safe remembering that event because now you have attached that memory to someone who loves you, accepts you, and would protect you if necessary.

Shame is a complex emotion to process and a powerful emotion to harbor, but it is life-changing to overcome. There is no memory too deeply rooted or experience too traumatic to heal. You are not forever defined by the words someone spoke to you decades ago. When your tormentor is unmasked, you will find that you were an equal match for him the entire time.

You can find a counselor to process past trauma and shame with, if that is something you would like to do. You may consult the online catalog of counselors to find someone to meet with. The reception team can also help you if you would prefer. Contact the office today to learn more about how a therapist can help you overcome shame.

item.title: Relaxation Techniques for Anxiety: Getting Momentary Relief and Developing Lasting Calm
item.description:
It’s no secret that life is stressful and that it can be a challenge making it through the month in one piece. You might be anxious because you are living from one paycheck to the next, because you have to deal with relationship or parenting issues, because you have a difficult work project, or a combination of all of these things. While it may be helpful to find ways to cope in the present moment, you can also benefit from learning relaxation techniques for future anxiety.

Build an Anxiety Coping Toolbox

When a house is falling apart, a repair person will come and inspect each problem and the extent of the damage. From here, they will gather the necessary tools and materials and fix one problem at a time until the house is repaired. Working on your mental health is similar to fixing up a house. Many issues are connected, but you will only make progress when you focus on one problem at a time. Additionally, the job goes faster when you have a full toolbox.

When you fill your self-help toolbox with relaxation techniques for anxiety, you can learn to cope in anxious moments. Practicing coping effectively today can also help to build a foundation for peace and calm in the future. To fix the damage caused by anxiety, you must learn to surrender certain parts of your life while taking control of others. It’s not easy to know how to do, but you can begin learning today.

Quick Relaxation Techniques for Anxiety

It is difficult, and often feels impossible, to learn anything new until you have learned to de-escalate your anxiety in the moment. Luckily, there are many relaxation and focus exercises you can acquire to place in your self-help toolbox. When you find the most effective ones, you can practice them both when feeling calm and whenever your anxiety spikes.

Anxiety is not always linked to overthinking. Sometimes a feeling of dread and panic feels like it comes out of nowhere, escalating until you are sweating, out of breath, and your heart is racing. You can reduce the physical effects of anxiety by practicing breathing techniques and by focusing your attention on the outside world. It might take many attempts to complete these techniques. If you practice them consistently, you will find them becoming an automatic reaction to sudden anxiety.

Start by focusing on your breathing. When your nervous system goes into panic mode, your body floods with adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prime your body to face a threat or run from it, even when there is no threat. When you control your breathing with deep, steady inhale-exhale rhythms, your brain begins to calm as it realizes you are not in immediate danger and brings your nervous system back to its rest-and-digest mode.

There are different inhale-exhale rhythms you can try, and some will be more effective than others. A simple one to start with is inhaling through your nostrils, imagining your breath going down to your belly, slowly filling up your lungs to their capacity, holding the breath for three seconds, then slowly emptying your lungs by blowing through your mouth. Try to make the exhale longer than your inhale.

One of the most common and effective relaxation tips for anxiety is the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding method. This exercise helps you focus on the outside world as a distraction from your anxiety and an effective mindfulness practice. After taking a few cleansing breaths, find five things that you can see, four things that you can feel, three things that you can hear, two things that you can smell, and one thing that you can taste. Check in with yourself before and after, noticing the severity of your emotions.

When you focus on your five senses in this way, your parasympathetic nervous system becomes activated. Your body will automatically start to calm and come out of panic mode. Relaxation exercises like these are simple and are most effective when repeated over and over again. You can practice them daily in any location. Most importantly, they are an effective way to impact your anxiety immediately.

Changing How You Worry

While you may find tools that will help you calm down immediately, your anxiety will likely return. Relaxation techniques for anxiety must help your physical response to anxiety. This is the short-term coping method. Next, you need to find techniques that will help you cope with anxiety in the mid-term future. This involves addressing your mental state. Later, you will look at the emotional reasons you are anxious as a long-term way to cope with anxiety.

You know from experience that there is no on/off switch when it comes to worry. You also know that worry escalates to panic unless you keep it in check. An effective way to cope with worry is to allow yourself some time each day to worry about things.

For example, you could choose 5 p.m. each afternoon as your designated “Worry Time.” During Worry Time, give yourself ten to twenty minutes to ruminate on a single issue. You can be as dramatic or understated as you wish. If the issue pops into your head at any other time through your day, tell yourself that you will worry about it during Worry Time later, or tomorrow if it is late at night. It can be helpful to have a list to jot worries down for later.

Practice logging information about your anxiety. Whether you use a physical book or a note app on your phone, keep track of things like:

  • Where were you when you began to overthink?
  • What was the issue?
  • What started the panic session?
  • How did you respond to it?
  • How long did it last?

Over time, this record will show you the patterns and your progress surrounding anxiety, panic, and overthinking. This gives you further tools, like knowing what you need to avoid, what you need to focus more on, and some ideas of what is effective for you when you begin worrying.

You can better deal with anxiety in the mid-term by doing one helpful action a day. Pick an action that directly reduces your anxiety and be intentional in performing it daily. It could be checking in with a certain friend, going for a walk in a certain spot, having quiet time with your Bible and prayer journal, or whatever activity makes you feel comforted. When you perform one calming activity daily, you will make better decisions about how you handle stress in the future.

Dealing with Anxiety in the Long-term

When you have filled your self-help toolbox with tools that help you deal with anxiety in the moment and cope over time, you can turn your attention to dealing with anxiety for the future. Relaxation techniques for anxiety are only a single aspect of dealing with the bigger issue. There is deeper work to be done if you are going to get a handle on anxiety for good.

When you have developed a daily routine for handling anxiety, and when you have been consistent with practicing the techniques that help you, you might find that the anxiety has not disappeared. You have not failed. As frustrating as it is, you might have something unresolved that you need to deal with. Alternatively, you might have a medical issue that can be aided with medication. Either way, this is where you must seek outside help.

If you have never had a vulnerable conversation with someone, now could be the time to do it. It’s natural to be guarded about certain things. Many people feel embarrassed about having anxiety at all, even though it is not their fault. Your best chance at handling anxiety long-term is to find someone you can trust, and to begin having some honest conversations with them. You might find that what you needed most was to share a few burdens with someone who cares.

People often find that it’s easier to open up to a stranger than it is to their close friends. This is part of the reason counseling is so effective; you can share whatever you want with a professional listener who will keep your confidence. If you would like to meet with a counselor, reach out to us or consult the online catalog of counselors we host.

item.title: It Is Not Too Late: Parental Regret and Reconciliation
item.description:
Many parents experience moments of regret in their relationships with their children. It could be a harsh word spoken in anger, years of emotional distance that was never addressed, or a relationship with a child that slowly drifted into something unrecognizable. These are the kinds of things that stay. Regret over these moments is a weight that doesn’t fade, and for many parents, it quietly shapes every interaction that comes after.

Many adult children carry wounds that become part of how they move through the world. It’s hard to address parental regret and the hope of reconciliation in a single conversation or a grand gesture. It is a process, layered and complicated by grief, pride, and hidden pain.

Both parents and adult children need to move toward healing with intention. That kind of intentionality is harder than it sounds when the wounds run deep, and the history between them is long and complicated. Still, we can rest on the promise in Scripture: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NIV)

Understanding the Weight of Parental Regret

Parental regret extends beyond wishing things had gone differently. It carries a particular kind of anguish with the knowledge that the people most affected were children who had no choice in the matter. That weight often shows up as a sense of helplessness, as though a parent feels trapped in an identity they can’t escape. And for many, that feeling doesn’t go away on its own.

This is similar to moral injury, which occurs when emotional damage stems from the gap between who a person wanted to be and who they actually were. That type of shame lingers long after the moment has passed. Most parents manage it privately rather than address it directly. That isolation only deepens the wound over time.

Parental regret is especially complex because of its intersection with love. Loving someone and knowing you caused them harm produces a grief that is hard to name. It shows up as depression, as anger turned inward, or as a quiet belief that repair is no longer possible.

Parents in these situations find themselves maneuvering between the desire to reach out and the fear that doing so will only cause more damage. That leaves the relationship stuck in a painful place, where both individuals carry wounds that were never named out loud. But God knows, and we can invite Him into our pain. “Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts.” (Psalm 139:23, NIV)

The Emotional Landscape of Adult Children in Parental Regret and Reconciliation

The decision to address parental regret and reconciliation is not simple for adult children. It involves navigating painful memories, weighing the emotional cost of restoration, and sitting with feelings that don’t have easy answers. Adult children often grieve for the parent they needed and the relationship they never had. Both of those things are true at the same time. Both deserve space rather than a rush to resolution.

Reconciliation doesn’t automatically restore what was broken. It requires trust, and trust takes time to rebuild. The idea of opening the door again often feels like a risk for adult children who have tried before without anything changing.

There is also a quiet social pressure to forgive quickly or to minimize what happened to preserve family harmony. That pressure produces reconciliation that looks good but is far from the real thing. When an adult child goes through the motions without genuine safety or acknowledgment, it can deepen the wound rather than begin to close it.

Christian counselors emphasize that there is no way to manufacture or hurry genuine reconciliation. It is only reached through an intentional choice free from manipulation or guilt, and grounded in honesty about what happened. Scripture helps us in this: “Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.” (Colossians 3:13, NIV) This shows us how to handle these hard situations.

What Makes Parental Regret and Reconciliation Possible

The reconciliation that happens between a parent and a child does not come from both parties pretending the past didn’t occur. It only takes shape when both people are willing to face it honestly, with genuine acknowledgment of harm, rather than an apology offered to relieve personal guilt. Accountability forms the foundation of repair. It only holds when someone chooses to face what they did without deflecting.

When a parent takes responsibility without minimizing, without deflecting, and without asking the adult child to move faster than they are ready, it gives the adult child permission to be exactly where they are. That can feel vulnerable for the parent who doesn’t know how that honesty will land.

Faith plays a significant role in this process for families. Biblically, there is a call toward reconciliation rooted in truth and grace, not a mandate to ignore boundaries or overlook pain. Christian counselors help families understand that forgiveness and reconciliation are related but not the same.

Forgiveness can begin in the heart long before reconciliation is possible. Sometimes reconciliation has to wait until safety is established. When both take root, the result is a relationship that is more honest and grounded than what existed before. Jesus put a high value on reconciliation.

“Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift.” – Matthew 5:23-24, NIV

Mental Health, Faith, and the Journey Toward Healing

Repairing a parent-child relationship has a deep impact on mental health that is hard to keep hidden. The emotional work involved isn’t always easy to see from the outside. Depression, anxiety, and difficulty forming attachments in adulthood connect back to unresolved relational wounds. This is particularly true when those wounds go all the way back to the earliest relationships a person ever had.

The way parents connect with children at a young age is a big influence on the ability of the child to develop emotional regulation and experience intimacy throughout their lives. Because of this, the stakes of parental regret and reconciliation extend beyond the family unit. Moving toward reconciliation isn’t just about repairing one relationship. Reconciliation focuses on reclaiming and healing something that was hurt long ago.

Parents who grapple with regret find that the mental health implications run just as deep. Chronic guilt and shame, when left unaddressed, lead to withdrawal, self-isolation, and a diminished sense of personal worth. Parents carry an internal picture of what a good parent looks like. When they believe they missed that mark, it builds a kind of trap that doesn’t open easily without the support of a therapeutic relationship.

Shame does not have to be the outcome. When parents find their way into a space where their story can be heard without judgment, that cycle can begin to shift. It doesn’t happen overnight. But it does happen.

Christian counselors work at the intersection of faith and clinical support. That combination matters here because this kind of healing rarely happens without both.

Pursuing Healing

Reconciliation does not erase what happened or negate the pain that came from it. It is a painfully slow and tender decision to build something new from the rubble of what fell apart. Everyone involved must show up with honesty, patience, and a willing heart – and stay present even when it gets uncomfortable.

Not every relationship heals completely. That does not mean anyone has failed. It means grace is still needed. For those who take the first steps toward addressing parental regret and reconciliation, the healing potential is real. Scripture teaches us that grace goes beyond what any of us can accomplish alone. Something new can take place even in the middle of the chaos of regret and reconciliation.

And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose. – Romans 8:28, NIV

If you are facing the challenge of reconciliation and carrying a weight of regret, you do not have to navigate it alone. The first step toward something better is reaching out. Contact our reception team to learn more about parental regret and reconciliation and to get connected with a counselor who understands the complexities of family relationships.

item.title: Great Active Listening Examples to Model for Your Kids
item.description:
The technology bug has bitten everyone, leaving us all in a constant state of distraction and lack of focus, which is why you need great active listening examples to model for your kids. Active listening basically involves giving full attention to the speaker, understanding their message, and responding thoughtfully.

Technology has significantly hindered active listening skills in many of us, and it’s worse for young kids who are growing up with few good active listening examples to learn from. Kids these days see everyone all around them constantly glued to their smartphone, laptop, or television.

If you meet groups of young kids of late, you’re more likely to see everyone engaged in their gadgets rather than looking at each other or physically engaging. This makes it difficult to focus on conversations and actively listen.

With this kind of environment, it has become of paramount importance for every parent or guardian to make sure they help kids take tech breaks and learn active listening skills.

Other Ways Technology Impacts Active Listening

Multitasking Technology encourages multitasking, which can divide attention and reduce the ability to listen effectively.

Reduced Face-To-Face Interaction With the rise of digital communication, face-to-face interactions have decreased, limiting opportunities to develop active listening skills, which are more effectively honed in person.

Over Reliance on Visual Cues Video calls and virtual meetings often lead to an overreliance on visual cues, which can sometimes overshadow the importance of listening to the actual content being spoken.

Shortened Attention Spans The fast-paced nature of digital content, such as short videos and instant updates, has contributed to shorter attention spans and is less in tune with how to stay engaged in longer, more in-depth conversations.

Lack of Non-Verbal Feedback Digital communication lacks non-verbal cues such as body language or facial expressions that are crucial for active listening, and this leads to a lack of empathy in conversations and misunderstandings.

Environmental Noise Using technology in noisy environments, such as public places or background noise from other devices, can interfere with the ability to focus on the conversation.

Encouraging active listening in kids who are often on their gadgets can be challenging, but it’s possible with some creative strategies.

Great Active Listening Examples to Model for Kids

The Monkey-See-Monkey-Do Approach: Kids often mimic adult behavior, so you need to adopt a monkey-see-monkey-do approach by showing them practical active listening examples. Show them how it’s done by maintaining eye contact, nodding, and responding appropriately when they speak.

The Gadget-Free Family Time Approach: Set clear boundaries with specific times for gadget use and times for family interaction. This helps kids understand when it’s time to focus on physical listening and engaging with others. You can instead include board games, outdoor activities, or simply talk about your day.

The Fun Listening Game Approach: Engage in fun listening activities with your kids by incorporating games that require active listening, like:

  • Simon Says: A classic listening game that encourages kids to listen carefully to instructions.
  • Guess the Sound is a game where you make different sounds and have your child guess what they are.
  • Listen and Build: A game where you give timed, verbal instructions to build something with blocks or Legos.

The Bring-Back Story Time Approach: Revive the age-old family activity of reading stories together and have kids retell their stories and ask each other questions about the plot and characters. This encourages kids to listen actively and think about what they hear.

By incorporating these strategies, you can help your child feel involved and valued, promoting better listening habits and developing strong active listening skills even in a gadget-filled world.

If you or your kids are struggling with how to break away from the bad habits you have ingrained in yourselves that are hindering healthy, active listening, you might need to consider counseling.

Counselors can provide one-on-one sessions tailored to a child’s specific needs and help you identify and address any underlying issues that may be affecting their listening skills. Counseling provides a safe and supportive environment where children feel heard and valued. This encourages them to open up and practice active listening without fear of judgment.

A professional can also help identify and address any behavioral issues that may be hindering a child’s ability to listen actively, including managing distractions, reducing anxiety, or improving focus. Technology is great, but don’t let it take over your home and turn you all into strangers. Call us today and get professional help.

item.title: Why Am I So Angry All the Time? Practical Tips to Overcome Anger
item.description:
The Heart Angle

It is important to discuss anger from a heartfelt perspective, although anger is not known for being a heartfelt emotion. When a person asks why they are so angry all the time, the root cause may not be known, so the question will only be partially answered.

The root cause for a great deal of the anger that is experienced derives from issues or matters of the heart. There is a saying that says there is a thin line between love and hate. Indeed, it is so thin that at times their distance from one another is small.

As a therapist, I have found that when anger is unpacked, it often stems from heartbreak caused by disappointment, loss, grief, lack of progress, feelings of failure, rejection, abandonment, and even a lack of felt love. Anger is often telling you what you are avoiding.

Emotions are the byproduct of the deeper symptoms. What is going on in your heart that is portraying itself as anger? To answer this question, we must go underneath. Your anger is trying to tell you something. The question is: what? This is often what is occurring.

  • There is hurt without clarity.
  • Undealt-with rejection.
  • Unhealed abandonment.
  • You may be feeling powerless.
  • You may be feeling ignored.
  • You may have tolerated something for too long.
  • You may be feeling stuck.
  • You may even be angry because there is a truth somewhere in your life that you have been unwilling or unable to confront.

Take the time to consider each thought. Allow it to sit with you.

Anger and Our Relationship with the Truth

I believe a great deal of anger can be connected to our relationship with truth. Sometimes we are angry because we cannot tell the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we do not want to face the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we are not living according to what we know is true.

Then there are times when we are angry because someone else told us the truth and we were not ready to hear it. The truth can be uncomfortable. Truth can seem threatening. Truth can even seem insulting without the intention of being so.

Maybe you continue saying yes to people when you really want to push back. Yet the deeper problem may not be that people keep asking. The deeper problem may be that you have not been honest about what you can handle. You have trouble admitting your limitations, and you would rather die than have anyone perceive a weakness.

Perhaps you are angry about your lack of professional progression. You are feeling overlooked by your superiors and undervalued. You resent your coworkers for getting what you deserve. You used to love your company and once saw a future there. But now you dread work mornings. Deep down, you know it is time to make a change, but fear has prevented you from making a change.

Truth will also require you to acknowledge when you have participated in your own frustration. There are times when we remain in situations long after we know something must change. Nevertheless, we become angry with people for crossing boundaries we have never verbalized or enforced.

We may even become irritated when others do not recognize needs that we have never expressed. Standing toe to toe with truth means asking yourself what part of the situation belongs to you. That moment may be uncomfortable, but it can help show us where we still have the power to move differently.

Your anger is real. But so is the hurtful and hard-to-face truth underneath it. Jesus said that the truth would make us free. Freedom has never begun with pretending. Freedom requires us to become willing to see what is there. Sometimes anger increases because we are fighting reality that we feel helpless to change.

Think About It, You May Not Be Angry About Today

A major reason why anger can feel disproportionate is that the current situation is carrying the weight of several previous situations. Someone does something tiny, and in return you respond enormously. Ever wonder when you became so upset? The other person may wonder the same thing.

The answer could be that you were not only responding to what happened today, because that is all you can see in the moment. However, you neglected to really comprehend that you were responding to every time you felt overlooked. Not to mention every time you were disappointed, or for each time a promise was broken, or for each conversation that went unresolved.

Think about it, you may not be angry about today, but for every moment you have decided not to say anything. Your anger had been accumulating when experiences that you had in your life were not properly processed. This is why it is not unusual to encounter some people going from zero to one hundred over something that appears insignificant.

The current situation may simply be the final place where everything else came to a head. In those intense moments, ask yourself, “What else am I responding to right now?” The answer could separate today’s frustration from yesterday’s wound.

Practical Tips to Overcome Anger

The goal of overcoming anger is not to become a person who never gets angry. This is unrealistic and not maintainable. The key to overcoming anger is learning how to recognize what your anger is revealing before it begins attempting to take center stage. Your anger becomes more manageable when you have practical steps that can help you move from reacting to your anger toward understanding it and responding differently.

Identify what is happening beneath the anger Instead of “I am upset,” finish the sentence: “I am angry because I felt…” Permit yourself to go above and beyond what may have been your obvious answer. Were you feeling ashamed? Did you feel disregarded? Did you feel powerless? Remember, naming what is at the root of your anger will aid you in understanding what really needs your attention,

Start separating what you can change from what you cannot control Ask: “What am I avoiding?” You may already know what needs to be changed. The hard part may be accepting what that truth may require from us.

Do not shut down speaking what you feel sooner Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. You cannot control another person’s choices. You can control what you participate in. You can decide what you will tolerate. You can also determine what access someone will continue to have to you.

Examine your expectations Determine what was conveyed. Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. Learn to communicate frustration while it is still frustration. Not everything requires confrontation, but important matters should not continually be buried.

Decide what you should be grieving instead of correcting Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. You may be trying to get an apology you will never receive or attempting to change something that has already happened. Grief may be necessary where correction is no longer possible.

Choose what your anger will yield Let it lead to a boundary, conversation, decision, healing work, or change rather than damage. Anger has energy attached to it. Decide where that energy will go. Your anger can destroy something or reveal what needs to be different. The responsibility is deciding what happens next.

item.title: True Transformation: Rewiring the Brain with Healthy Thoughts
item.description:
Have you ever thought, “I want transformation but don’t know how to achieve it”? Or “Why am I not experiencing lasting change?” Have you tried hard to make some changes in your life, but you still feel little to no progress? Or maybe you experienced some good changes, but they did not last long? What is the key to authentic and lasting transformation? The answer is in our thoughts.

The Garden Image

Let me explain with an image. Imagine your mental health is a large garden. The goal is to keep the garden flourishing with good plant life, which will represent mental health wellness. Now imagine the problem you are facing is a standard garden weed. The weed is toxic to your garden and must be removed. The weed can be anxiety, anger outbursts, depression, addiction, trauma, relationship discord, etc.

Removing the weed will keep away significant damage to your mental health. Some people will attempt to fix the problem by removing the stems and leaves and anything else they can see above the soil. They walk away thinking, “The weed is gone, so the problem is solved.” But they return in a few months to find that the same garden weed returned with more leaves and stems. How could it possibly have grown back?

As you can guess, the roots of the weed remained in the soil, which only made the problem appear to be gone. The person failed to pull the garden weed out by the roots. As long as the roots remain, the problem remains, which means no real lasting change can take place.

Now let me give some explanation of what the different parts of the weed represent. The stems and leaves of the garden weed represent behaviors and feelings. The roots of the garden weed represent our thoughts.

Understandably, we focus on the behaviors quite a bit to fix the problem because it is what we are seeing. Behaviors are everything from substance use and running away to playing and laughing. We can try to change our behaviors and feelings all day long but still have no real lasting change. Psychology teaches us that our thoughts affect our emotions and then our emotions affect our behaviors, and then our behaviors create our experiences.

So, for authentic and lasting change to take place, we need to examine the thoughts because they are the root, the epicenter, of everything that is happening. We must examine the deepest part of ourselves because this holds the greatest power to affect our entire psyche. This means that (in this image) the root of the weed needs to be fully removed in order for there to be change.

But it does not stop there. Not only does the root of the weed need to be removed, but it also needs to be replaced with a far healthier plant (a healthier thought). When we have healthy thoughts, incredible, lasting transformation starts to take place.

Rewiring the Brain

So now that we understand that the root of the garden weed is toxic thoughts (untruthful, unhelpful, distorted thinking), what do we do about it? The answer is in rewiring the brain.

God created our brains in a way to have the ability to remap and rewire themselves. Romans 12:2 states, “Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” In today’s world, we know this concept formally as neuroplasticity and cognitive restructuring.

Neuroplasticity is the remarkable ability of the nervous system to change, adapt, and reorganize its physical structure and functional connections throughout your life. It is the biological mechanism that allows the brain to learn new skills, recover from injuries, and adapt to changing environments.

This means that the transformation we seek doesn’t begin with changing circumstances or relationships. Transformation starts in our minds. We must shift the way we think in order to get the transformation we want. So, let’s begin by understanding some basic neuroscience.

Every time you have a thought, a neural pathway is created or reused in your brain. The more you have a particular thought, the stronger that neural pathway becomes and eventually becomes an automatic thought. Automatic thoughts are pathways in our mind that we have used so many times that they are instantly the way we think about a certain situation, person, or stimulus.

The first thing to do is to record these thoughts, formally known as a Thought Record. In the world of cognitive behavioral therapy, we call this cognitive restructuring. We select one thought at a time and put it on trial to challenge its validity. We ask, “Is this true? Is this hurting me or helping me? Is this thought based on objective facts?” When we find that a thought is untruthful, distorted, and only hurting us, we can then identify that as a toxic thought.

Once we have identified a toxic thought, we then select a replacement thought that is truthful, healthy, and helpful. God, being the divine architect of our brains, knows that the way to fix toxic thinking is by deliberately focusing our thoughts on what is healthy and helpful. Philippians 4:13 instructs us to focus our thoughts on what is true, noble, right, pure, lovely, admirable, excellent, and praiseworthy.

And again, science is just now catching up to this. Neuroscience proves Philippians 4:13 by showing us how new neural pathways form when we have a thought. Studies and research conclude that healthy, helpful thoughts bring life and wellness to our bodies.

The antidote to toxic thinking is to intentionally focus on and rehash thoughts that are true, noble, right, pure, lovely, admirable, excellent, and praiseworthy. This is the game changer. So, the only way to make that toxic thought stop is to replace it with a new thought.

Now the next part takes discipline and practice. We live in a culture of fast-paced results, but our brain does not operate in the same way. Our brain needs significant repetition to wire in an automatic thought. The studies and research on neuroplasticity have found that the new thought needs to be rehearsed enough to get wired into the brain.

In one study, participants were directed to rehearse their new healthy thought by taking five minutes every day to repeat the healthy thought out loud or write it down over and over again. The results showed that many participants had successfully rewired their brain with the new healthy thought by day sixty-three. The toxic thought naturally eased in intensity, and for many, the toxic thought ceased.

The new wiring of healthy thought results in more positive emotions (peace, optimism, contentment) and then creates more desired behaviors (restful sleep, connecting with others, responding calmly to stress). This is what we want in our mental health garden. Pulling out weeds and then planting healthy plants is the key to lasting change.

Remember, your life will not change until your mind changes. You are only limited by how you see yourself and how you choose to think. Your mind and thoughts are the game changer to true and lasting transformation.

How To Rewire Your Mind

Write down all your thoughts (a Thought Record)

Put your thoughts on trial Determine whether it is healthy, helpful, and truthful, or untruthful, hurtful, and toxic.

To help determine if the thought is healthy or toxic, ask the following: Is this based on facts? What are the objective facts here? Did I confirm that my interpretation is based on reality? Did the person actually say that to me? Is there another way I could look at this? Did that actually happen? Does this thought make me feel worse, or does it make things feel more manageable?

Select a new healthy thought

Working on this with a therapist or good friend is always helpful because they can offer a new way of thinking about this thought that you likely have not considered before.

Meditate on this new thought through active repetition every day Reserve five minutes every day to rehearse the new healthy thought by saying it out loud or writing it. Continue this routine until the new thought becomes an automatic thought. Anticipate about two months to notice real change and a transformation that lasts a lifetime.

Repeat this process with every toxic thought This is a lifelong skill to commit to.

Example

The automatic thought: “I can’t do anything right.”

Challenge the thought with questions: What exactly do I feel I have not done right? Is it really true that everything I have done is wrong? Is this thought hurting me or is it helping me?

Consider the answers: This thought makes me feel bad, which means it is hurting me. No, it is not true that everything I have done is wrong. I have indeed done a few things wrong because my coworker verbally told me that I did not complete certain tasks needed before closing the shop. But there are a lot of things I have done correctly at work. I know this because my supervisor thanked me for the good work.

Select a new healthy thought: “Sometimes I make mistakes. I am human, I am not perfect, and mistakes are part of life. There are a lot of things I do correctly. I can choose to learn from my mistakes.”

item.title: The Benefits of Sleep and Why We Need It
item.description:
Studies have found that the benefits of sleep go beyond just giving your body and brain a rest from the stimuli and rigors of the day. It is a biological necessity. Certain processes vital to your health and well-being can only happen when your body powers down and you are asleep.

It is a common experience that a problem difficult at night is resolved in the morning after the committee of sleep has worked on it. – John Steinbeck

Sleep supports brain function, physical recovery, and immune system function by providing a period of quietness. This is one of the biggest benefits of sleep. It enables the brain to reset and restore its connections and carry out important processes. These involve memory consolidation, hormone regulation, tissue repair, and the restoration of energy.

Without enough quality sleep, your body and brain are unable to function properly. This can affect your mood and emotional well-being, concentration, judgment, reaction time, and ability to think clearly. It can also increase the risk of chronic health problems such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

How Sleep Works

Sleep is an active process that consists of four distinct stages that a healthy person cycles through multiple times during the night. Each stage plays an essential part in the cycle that enables your brain and body to recover and grow. This helps you wake up refreshed and ready to face the day ahead.

Stage 1 (N1): N1 is the first and lightest stage of sleep and is easy to wake up from. It is a dozing off, transition period that only happens when you first fall asleep, and typically lasts just a few minutes. During this phase, heartbeat and breathing start to slow, muscles relax, and you may experience occasional sensations of falling as you start to nod off.

Stage 2 (N2): N2 is the longest sleep stage, making up roughly 45-55% of your total sleep time. It is a light to moderate phase during which your body temperature drops, muscles relax more deeply, heart rate and breathing slow, eye movement stops, and brain waves slow down. The brain has short bursts of activity that some researchers believe happen as it reorganizes memories and information gleaned while you were awake.

Stage 3 (N3): N3, also known as deep, slow-wave, or delta sleep, is the deepest sleep stage. Your body is the most relaxed during this stage, and it is the hardest one to wake up from. This is the restorative phase of sleep.

During N3, growth and other hormones critical to the repair and rebuilding of your body and mind are released into your bloodstream, strengthening your immune system and enabling tissue repair as your body heals and grows. Even though brain activity is reduced during this stage, some studies show that deep, delta wave sleep contributes to creativity, insightful thinking, and memory.

Stage 4 (REM Sleep): REM sleep is where most dreaming takes place. Brain activity increases to close to what it is when you are awake. Your eyes move rapidly behind your eyelids, and voluntary muscles such as your arms, legs, and torso become temporarily immobilized. This is to protect you from physically acting out vivid dreams and potentially injuring yourself.

During the night, you may go through several sleep cycles. Most typically, people go through four to six of them. Not all are the same length, but on average, they tend to last about 90 minutes.

Benefits of Sleep

In addition to boosting your energy and alertness by providing you with an extended period of stillness and reduced activity, sleep enables several essential physical and psychological functions to take place that cannot happen in the body’s awake state.

Restoration and Repair: During sleep, the brain clears out waste products and neurotoxins that accumulate throughout the day. It also releases hormones necessary for body tissues to be able to grow and repair themselves.

Improved Executive Function: Healthy sleep improves executive functions such as sound judgment and decision-making. It improves your ability to recognize and react appropriately to danger and threats.

Problem-Solving: As neurotoxins are cleared from the brain during sleep, cognitive functions such as logical reasoning are enhanced. Studies have shown that when facing a complicated problem, sleep often improves your chances of finding a creative solution to it when you wake up.

Memory Consolidation: Sleep enables the brain to organize, categorize, and consolidate memories and learned information so they take root. This boosts memory and makes it easier to access and use things you learn, increases attention span, and improves focus and concentration.

Emotional Regulation: Sleep reduces irritability and anxiety, improves your mood, and helps you regulate your emotions. This occurs by enabling you to better handle the physical and emotional effects of stress.

Strengthened Immune System: Adequate sleep strengthens immune function, enhances your immune system’s ability to identify potential threats, and increases your body’s ability to fight off disease and infections.

Improved Heart Health and Reduced Inflammation: Sleep slows down your heart rate, lowers blood pressure, reduces inflammation, and decreases your risk of stroke or cardiovascular disease.

Improved Metabolism: Getting enough sleep helps improve your metabolism, which promotes blood sugar control, reduces the risk of diabetes, and helps you maintain a healthy weight.

Enhances Athletic Performance: Adequate sleep facilitates tissue repair, cell regeneration, and muscle growth, and contributes to enhanced endurance, alertness, and response time.

Effects of Sleep Deprivation

Sleep deprivation can affect your mood, reduce your ability to control your emotions, impair your judgment, and hurt your mental health and physical well-being.

In addition to causing you to feel tired or sluggish during the day, insufficient sleep makes it harder to focus, think clearly, or remember information. It also decreases your attention span and ability to make sound decisions. A lack of sleep can lead to cloudy thinking that heightens your risk of making costly mistakes or becoming involved in an accident.

If allowed to become persistent and long-term, sleep deprivation can weaken your immune system. This can increase your susceptibility to sickness and chronic health issues such as cardiovascular disease or diabetes. Extended sleep deprivation can also interfere with your metabolism, cause relationships to suffer, lead to depression and anxiety, and even shorten your life.

Tips for Getting a Good Night’s Sleep

  • Create and commit to a regular sleep schedule to help your body maintain a consistent internal clock.
  • Adopt a relaxing bedtime routine that helps you wind down before bed and make it easier to fall asleep.
  • As much as possible, go to bed and get up at the same time every day – even on weekends or when on vacation.
  • Make your bedroom a comfortable, relaxing, soothing place, and keep it cool, dark, and quiet.
  • Stop using electronics and avoid screen time at least an hour before bed.
  • Store digital devices somewhere other than your bedroom.
  • Keep naps short, and avoid napping late in the day.
  • Get exposure to at least 20 minutes of natural light first thing in the morning.
  • Exercise regularly, preferably early in the day.
  • Avoid late-night snacking.
  • Avoid using alcohol, nicotine, or caffeine late in the day or before bed.
  • If you can’t fall asleep, don’t try to force it. Instead, try picking up a book and reading until you start to feel sleepy.

Benefits of Sleep Therapy

If you have been having trouble falling or staying asleep and getting the rest you need, you may want to consider sleep therapy. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), in particular, is an effective non-drug treatment that addresses the root causes of your struggles with sleep rather than just the symptoms.

CBT-I helps you identify negative thought patterns and behaviors that may be contributing to your difficulties and retrain your brain to replace them with new ones that support better sleep. This can be explored with a trained therapist like those in this office.

If you would like to set up an appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors at our location, please give us a call. Your first appointment is risk-free.
